title: The Foot She Almost Stepped On
tease: She has won, and she cannot stop. So he lies down in front of her, in the middle of it, and waits to see whether she looks down.

source.work: Devī Māhātmya; and the later tellings
source.traditionNote: The Devī Māhātmya gives Kālī her arrival and her battles, and stops there. The scene everyone actually pictures — her unable to stop, Śiva lying down in her path — is carried by later Purāṇic tellings and by living tradition rather than by those chapters. It is also the reason she is painted the way she is.
checkedAgainst: Devī Māhātmya — Coburn, 'Encountering the Goddess', SUNY
Kinsley, 'Hindu Goddesses' — on the iconography and its sources

sourcing.locus: Devī Māhātmya 5–11; Mahiṣāsura dies in ch. 3

variants.differs: Whether the stopping is in the text at all
variants.tellings: The Devī Māhātmya has Kālī fight and win and says nothing about a dance that would not end. The scene is told across later Purāṇic material and, more than anywhere, in Bengali and Tamil practice.
variants.weTell: The later scene, with the join marked — because it is what every painting of her is of.

variants.tellings: Usually she has bitten it in shock at what her foot has landed on. Some tellings make it the blood-drinking; some make it plain ferocity.
variants.weTell: The shock, which is the reading that makes the story about stopping rather than about winning.

variants.differs: Where the out-thrust tongue comes from
variants.tellings: The Devī Māhātmya already gives her a lolling tongue when she arrives, chapters before any Śiva-underfoot scene exists. The later tradition explains the same feature as shock at what her foot has landed on.
variants.weTell: The later explanation, and we say that the oldest text had the tongue there first — which is a good argument that the scene was built to explain the picture, rather than the picture painted from the scene.

audience.careNote: A battlefield, told at a distance but not softened: an asura who copies himself from his own spilt blood, and a goddess who drinks it before it can land so that he cannot. Nobody is tortured and there is no dwelling on wounds, but the drinking is in the text and is in the story. The end is quiet.

blocks.text: Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa came onto the field with their army, and «Durgā» looked at them and got angry, and «Kālī» came out of her forehead already holding everything she needed.
She was made for a job. The job was «Raktabīja».

His name means blood-seed, and it is a description. Every drop of his blood that touched the ground stood up as another one of him. So every sword-stroke made the problem worse, and the army had been doing that all morning, and there were thousands of him by the time anyone worked out what was happening.

Kālī did the only thing that works. She did not wound him more carefully. She caught the blood before it could land — drank it out of the air — and the copies with it, until there were none of him left anywhere.
And that was the end of the battle.
But it was not the end of Kālī.

She was still going. The field was empty and she was still going, and the ground was taking it, and nobody could get near enough to say anything to her, and the gods stood at the edge of it and understood that nobody had any way of turning this off.
So «Śiva» walked out into the middle of it and lay down.
He did not fight her. He did not hold anything up. He lay down in her path, on the ground, where she was going to come next, and waited to find out whether she would look down.
Her foot came down on his chest. And she looked.
In every painting you have ever seen of her, her tongue is out. This is the moment people point to for it.
Though the oldest book already gives her that tongue on the day she arrives — so the picture may have come first, and the scene been built to explain it.
Told this way it is not fierceness. It is a person biting their tongue at what they have just done.
Everyone had been frightened of what she would do to the enemy. What actually frightened them was what she did once there wasn't one.
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa came onto the field with their army, and «Durgā» looked at them and got angry.

Not the ordinary kind. The text says her face went black with it, and out of her forehead came «Kālī» — already there, already armed, holding a sword and a noose and wearing what she wears, needing nothing explained to her.
She was made for a job, and the job had a name.
«Raktabīja». It means blood-seed, and it is not a title, it is a description of the problem.
Every drop of his blood that reached the ground stood up as another one of him. Full size. Fully armed. Exactly as difficult as the original.
So the harder the army fought him, the more of him there was. Every cut made two. They had been at it all morning, doing the sensible thing, and the sensible thing was manufacturing the enemy.
By the time anybody understood what was happening, the field was full of him. Thousands. All the same. All coming.
Kālī did not fight him more carefully. That was never going to work and she did not try it.

She caught the blood before it could land. Out of the air, before it reached the ground, so that the ground never got the chance to make anything of it — and the copies that were already standing, she took those too, until there was nothing of him anywhere and nothing left to make more from.
It is the only thing that works on a problem shaped like that, and the text says so plainly and does not dress it up.
And that was the end of the battle.
It was not the end of Kālī.
This is the part the older chapters do not tell you and everybody knows anyway. She did not stop. The field was empty — no enemy, nobody left to fight, nothing to do — and she was still going.
The ground took the shock of it. Then the ground began to have trouble taking it.
And the gods who had been so relieved an hour earlier stood at the edge of the field and worked out, slowly, that nothing they had was any use here.
She had not come out of them. She had come out of the Devī, and she was not theirs to call back.
Nobody could go near her. There was no sentence anyone could say from that distance that would arrive.
So «Śiva» walked out into the middle of it and lay down on the ground.
Not fighting her. Not holding anything up, not blocking, not shouting her name. He lay down in her path — in the place she was going to come next — and waited to find out whether she would look down.
Which is the most frightening thing anybody does in any of these stories, and he does it lying still.
Her foot came down on his chest.
And she looked down.
In every painting you have ever seen of her — and you have seen them, on calendars, on shop walls, over doorways — her tongue is out.
That is the moment people point to for it — though the oldest book already gives her that tongue on the day she arrives, which is worth knowing.

Told this way it is not a taunt. It is what a face does when it has just understood what it has done: the tongue caught between the teeth, the way people here still do when they have knocked something over.
She stopped.
And then there was a field with nobody moving on it, and a great many gods a long way off, not saying anything, working out what to do with their faces.

Nobody thanked him. The tellings do not have anyone thank him. He gets up, and she is herself again, and the story goes back to the war it was in the middle of, and the thing he did is left lying there for whoever notices.
She had won. Winning was never the hard part. Stopping was the hard part, and somebody had to lie down in front of her before she could do it.

linked.reason: the same Devī, an earlier war, and the nine nights people count at Navarātri

close.question: Śiva did not try to stop her by being stronger. He lay down. When somebody you know is too upset to hear you, what actually works?
close.seed: Stopping is its own skill, and it is not the same skill as winning.

ifTheyAsk.q: Is it wrong that she drank his blood?
ifTheyAsk.a: It is meant to be shocking, and softening it would make nonsense of the story — Raktabīja could not be beaten by any decent method, and she is what arrives when decent methods have run out. What the story does next is the part worth noticing: it does not celebrate her. It shows everyone else frightened, and unable to do anything about it, because she did not come out of them.

The story does not say, which is its own answer. He does not do anything clever — no weapon, no argument, no trick. He makes himself the one thing she cannot walk over without seeing. If he had been wrong about her, the story would have ended very differently, and everyone telling it knows that.

ifTheyAsk.q: Why is her tongue out in the pictures?
ifTheyAsk.a: This story is the explanation, and it is why the image is everywhere. Some tellings say the tongue is about the blood and some say it is plain ferocity. The version told here — that she has bitten her tongue in shock at where her foot has landed — is the one that makes the picture a picture about stopping rather than about winning.
